extracted.intended_audience: event organizers, aspiring/new and established cartoonists, writers, and general audiences interested in humor and creativity
extracted.subtask_description: A set of public-speaking and workshop topics about creating cartoons and captions, understanding what makes people laugh, applying humor in professional settings, and techniques to increase creativity (including use of AI/big data). Intended both as guidance for creators and as descriptions of talks for audiences/organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing a successful New Yorker cartoon
rubrics_metrics.description: “writing a successful New Yorker cartoon” — Mankoff’s presentations largely focus on the creative process, from writing a successful New Yorker cartoon to inspiring creativity in others and enhancing ideas with A.I and big data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the soup-to-nuts process of cartoon creation, shows work of New Yorker artists, and offers concrete pointers on increasing odds of acceptance (e.g., understanding reader expectations, how cartoons are selected from thousands to ~15 per issue). Includes multimedia examples and analysis of why some cartoons “don’t get” and how to fix that.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposing your ideas, imagination & wit to enhance your creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Naked Cartoonist: Exposing Your Ideas, Imagination & Wit to Enhance Your Creativity” — a criterion emphasizing the deliberate cultivation and exposure of ideas, imagination, and wit as central to creative output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice includes finding personal voice, learning from masters, turning current events into comic material, practical techniques and anecdotes, and exercises designed to get past blocks (e.g., embracing unconventional routines such as naps or playful lies as creative fuel). Aimed at anyone staring at a blank page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find your own personal voice and message
rubrics_metrics.description: “how you can find your own personal voice and message” — cartoons and humor should reflect an identifiable personal voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mankoff stresses learning from past masters while developing originality; his talks and workshops include techniques and mentorship to help creators discover and refine their voice so work is distinct and marketable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform current events into comic material
rubrics_metrics.description: “how you can transform a current event into a comic tour-de-force” — topicality and the transformation of events into humorous insight is a craft goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance is given through examples and anecdotes showing how to convert news/events into cartoons that resonate, balancing timeliness with lasting comic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perseverance/volume of submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: “If at first you don’t succeed, try 2,000 times” / “It took three years and 2,000 submissions …” — persistence and submission volume are explicit requirements for success in cartoon publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mankoff uses his own history (over 2,000 early submissions, ~950 published cartoons) to argue that more than talent, steady practice and high submission volume increase chances of publication. Workshops emphasize treating creativity as a long-haul process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and match reader/audience expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting cartoons toward “the laughs readers expect” — successful cartoons must fit the magazine/audience’s sensibility and expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As Cartoon Editor he evaluated thousands weekly to select the few that fit The New Yorker’s voice; guidance includes learning what the publication’s (or audience’s) tone, subtlety level, and sensibility are and tailoring submissions or captions accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartoon caption craft for contests
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical criteria for crafting captions for the New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest — captions must compete in a crowdsourced environment and appeal to both editors and a broad voting readership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talks cover how the contest works (readers submit captions, editors pick three finalists, readers vote), what increases odds of winning (understanding what makes the crowd laugh), and includes live caption challenges so participants practice producing and selecting punchlines. Mankoff also partnered with algorithmic tools to analyze large caption datasets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lessons from crowdsourced humor
rubrics_metrics.description: “Crowdsourcing lessons in humor” — audience-selected punch lines reveal patterns about what makes people laugh and are a source of insights for creators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on millions of caption submissions and finalists selection, the lessons include empirical patterns (what crowds prefer), how to structure caption contests for engagement, and how to interpret crowd favorites vs. editorial picks. Includes sponsor-provided captionless cartoons, finalist selection, and on-stage competitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using AI and big data to augment creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrating algorithms and A.I. to enhance idea generation and to help cull funniest captions (e.g., partnerships with Microsoft and Google DeepMind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mankoff describes developing algorithms trained on millions of captions to surface promising submissions; talks and workshops show how big data and software (e.g., Botnik Studios tools) can augment — not replace — human creativity and curation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying humor effectively in professional contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: “Humor has three main benefits … blocks stress; makes us mentally flexible; serves as a social lubricant” — using humor strategically in workplaces and professions is a measurable objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Available talks tailor humor to professions (Humor and Law, Healthcare, Education, Business Executives, Mental Health). Guidance covers exercises and examples showing how humor can increase effectiveness, manage change, reduce stress, build rapport, and be used appropriately in different professional settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor in sales, marketing, and customer service
rubrics_metrics.description: “Six ways humor works with customers … creates rapport and overcomes sales resistance … customers remember that message better” — commercial effectiveness is a criterion for business humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talk covers why advertisers use humor, how humor creates involvement and recall, when humor is an icing vs. a relationship-saver, and how gender differences in humor affect strategy. Examples, videos, and cartoons illustrate appropriate use in advertising and customer interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curation and editorial selection skills
rubrics_metrics.description: “Analyzing, critiquing, and selecting each cartoon” — skill in critiquing and curating cartoons is a distinct professional standard for editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mankoff’s role involved mentoring artists, providing editorial feedback, and applying selection criteria to thousands of submissions weekly. Guidance includes how to critique constructively, mentor creators, and choose cartoons that fit editorial standards and reader expectations.
